beta_new: Mix of sport bolts and trad placements. South-facing provides good sun exposure. Straightforward climbing with consistent protection.

Helmet Butte is normally climbed as part of a Buck Creek Pass backpacking trip rather than a car-to-car day climb, given the ~17.6-mile round-trip approach. From a point at 5,600 ft on the Buck Creek Pass Trail ('Waypoint 86'), the recommended line turns off-trail toward Pass No Pass on a well-defined but braiding boot path, gains a notch around 7,200 ft below the summit block, then finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 3 scramble on solid rock, aiming for the block's south (left) side for the easiest line. An alternate line continues past the trail junction to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble - this option is likely hazardous when wet.
A simple, blocky line to a bolted anchor.

A boot path for Hibox leaves the main trail here (or at the second chute crossing) and climbs steeply but stays class 2 through timber to near treeline. Above the trees, go right around the first band of cliffs, then left around a rock outcrop, continue through more timber to a second cliff band, and take the gully on the right to gain the upper mountain. From there head right (east) along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side, which is climbed with a bit of class 3 near the top to reach the summit. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no continuous trail above the boot path.

moves.from: From the Rachel Lake trailhead, follow the maintained Rachel Lake Trail for roughly 2 miles to the first avalanche-chute clearing.

beta_new: First ascensionists Cooper, Denny, and the Fireys found the peak unpromising from either flanking notch, then located a class-4 route by following a ledge onto the north face that wasn't visible from below. The line is mostly scrambling with short steeper steps; conditions and difficulty vary considerably with season and snow coverage in the approach gully.

First climbed July 6, 2015 by Jason Schilling and Tim Halder, based out of a camp below the Chopping Block above Crescent Creek. The route climbs blocky ground low, a crux pitch 2 (5.10-) that leaves a dead-end dihedral and traverses left onto the face to a hand crack, moves through easier pitches, then tackles two more steep, run-out 5.8/5.10- faces higher on a distinct summit tower before an easy, loose finishing pitch. Rock quality was reported as predominantly solid to excellent higher on the face. Named after watching Spinal Tap's 'Stonehenge' scene at camp post-climb.

A steep snow couloir climb on the mountain's northeast aspect, reported by climbers as a direct, sustained line taking roughly 3 hours from upper Royal Lake Basin to the top of the couloir in good snow conditions. It sees a narrow seasonal window — climbed successfully in both an early-summer trip report and at least one winter ascent — and functions as the technical/snow-climbing counterpart to the standard rock scramble.

A moderate single-pitch sport climb that angles slightly left near the top to a chain anchor at the top of the cliff; the first bolted line established in the Spire Gully area, put up by its namesake honeymooning first-ascent party.

moves.value: Chain anchor at the top of the cliff
moves.from: to a chain anchor at the top of the cliff

beta_new: From the Libby Lake approach trail, climb a loose gully to gain Raven Ridge, then follow the ridge crest toward Hoodoo Peak. The first half of the ridge is easy class 2-3, but where it bends toward Hoodoo it steepens into sustained, exposed class 4 knife-edge scrambling. A roughly 10-ft overhanging step partway along requires either a solid 5.7 boulder-problem move or a short rappel to bypass; the final stretch to the Hoodoo summit eases back to class 2 boulders, with optional class 3-4 scrambling available along the ridge crest.

Most parties approach via the trail toward Libby Lake in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, then leave the trail to climb scree and boulder slopes toward Hoodoo Peak's summit ridge; the final stretch is mostly class 2 boulder-hopping with occasional easy class 3 moves.

From Sahale Glacier Camp (or a Horseshoe Basin camp), cross into Horseshoe Basin, gain the base of a class 3 dike/gully system below Ripsaw Ridge, and follow it (with a short class 4 step) up to the ridge crest near the 'Lick of Flame' spire. From there a narrow ramp leads to the summit; it begins as 3rd-class terrain and turns into a short section of 5th-class (5.2) climbing in its final ~100 ft below the top. Rope up for this last section — most parties treat it as one roughly 100-ft pitch.

moves.from: Descend by a single rappel off a horn on the summit (backed by old fixed webbing) or downclimb the same dike/ramp system, then retrace the approach.

beta_new: P1 climbs past bolts to chains at roughly 5.10+. P2 moves right and up a slab reported as possibly 5.12 and not freed as of 2015, so the pitch's grade and completion status are unresolved.

Begin at Lake Serene trailhead, ascend 2,000 feet through forest to the lake (4.1 miles), then climb steeply southeast toward the summit. The Hourglass Gully presents 40-60 degree snow and ice, with a crux 60-degree pitch on the East Ridge. The gully constricts dramatically near the exit with near-vertical sections. Timing is critical; the window for this route is narrow (early March through early May). After May, melted conditions expose loose rock and create severe bushwhacking challenges.

The route begins in a shallow, down-sloping depression with awkward climbing off two fixed pins, then follows the crest as directly as possible over several rock steps and across two significant notches to the summit, with the crux (5.9) typically encountered higher on the route. The climbing is of lower quality than on the Blue Buttress, and protection is hard to find in places. It is also notably longer than its neighbor — subsequent parties have reported as many as 12-17 roped pitches, and its character resembles the South Arete of South Early Winters Spire, stretched to over a thousand feet.

This is the line Tatum and Loudon took in 1904 and it remains the trade route on the North Peak. From a ridge camp near the border monument at roughly 6,300-6,400 ft, drop to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque, then climb the lower snowfield at an easy angle before the middle snowfield steepens enough to want crampons and an axe. Above the snow the route breaks onto loose Class 3 rock ramps and gullies, threading up and right to gain the northeast ridge crest. The ridge is generally Class 2-3, but around 7,600 ft a section of the connecting ledge has eroded away, leaving a short, badly exposed Class 4 traverse on loose, wet, dirty, down-sloping holds — the psychological crux of the climb. Above that it is attention-grabbing 4th class on sharp, unfractured Hozomeen chert to the summit block. The whole route is graded 'easy' and climbs nothing hard, but nothing on it is casual: the consensus across trip reports is that a fall is not survivable and the rock will not hold protection.

A climber reached roughly 60% of the route on a third try before retreating, free-climbing a crux pitch that earlier parties had aided. The second ascent, in 1998, involved a summit-day round trip of about 12 hours from bivouac back to the car. Treat all of this as thin, second-hand history rather than current beta.

A genuine Cascade backcountry big-wall problem rather than a route in the usual sense. The line takes the left-facing corner systems that lead directly to the summit, with rope-stretcher pitches through the 6-10 range and a leftward traverse of the wall's distinctive tiger-stripe ledges to avoid the overhanging upper section, reaching the summit ridge about 100 ft from the top. Twelve pitches, climbed all free at 5.9, with one shallow piton placed and removed and no bolts on the entire route - Cascade ground-up ethics applied to a wall that barely accepts hardware. The first ascensionists' own summary is the best warning available: the face is very large, much steeper than it appears from below, the rock is friable, and there are almost no protection cracks, even for thin pitons. One published account rates the line V 5.9+ R/X rather than the published IV 5.9, and the R/X reflects reality better than the number does. What the rock lacks in solidity and protection it partly returns in a plethora of in-cut features, which climb well where they are attached. Larson and Wehrly bivouacked atop pitch 10, about 100 m below the summit.

The historic first-ascent route. Scramble the ridge crest (Class 3/4, generally linking clumps of trees) over an intimidating Class 4 step to a false summit, downclimb into a notch (watch a loose block here), traverse a crumbly Class 2 ledge above a big cliff, then climb a blocky headwall to the summit block's east face. The crux is a short, well-protected, roughly 3-move low-5th (~5.3) curving dihedral just below the summit.

There is no true walk-up to Huckleberry's summit. The mountain's original (and for decades only) route climbs class 3-4 terrain along the ridge crest with a short, exposed low-5th-class step to top out the summit block; two later technical lines — a 5.7 South Face and a 5.6 West Face first climbed in 2001 — are more sustained rock routes. Nearly all parties, including strong scramblers, bring a rope and light rack to protect and rappel the final block.

A popular side trip from the Cascade Pass area or via the Ptarmigan Traverse. The south ridge route involves crossing a steep snow band and broken granite above Kool-Aid Lake, then class 2-3 scrambling with moderate exposure along the summit ridge. Route finding can be tricky; descend via the same route.

Climbs a steep face on good holds to a bolt guarding a thin finger-crack move, then finishes on horizontal cracks into an awkward but enjoyable left-facing corner. Mixed protection (3 bolts plus small-to-mid cams) makes it the trad line of the three Ice Box routes.

From Hannegan Pass, parties gain Ruth Mountain (via its glacier/snow slopes), then descend south and west from Ruth's summit toward a gully on its west side and continue down to the Ruth-Icy Saddle, from which Icy Peak is clearly visible. From the saddle, cross talus and slabs below a rock ridge onto Icy's glacier and climb firm snow to a notch just west of Icy's Northwest Spire, near 6,500 ft; from there, 2nd-3rd class climbing on mostly good rock leads to a 100-ft 4th-class summit gully and the Northwest summit, which holds the register. The true (Southeast) summit takes a harder, less often climbed line from the notch between the Northwest and Southeast summits up the Southeast Peak's steep, loose, very exposed Northwest Ridge to a Class 4 knife-edge summit ridge.

Most common Icy Peak route: from Hannegan Pass trailhead, ascend to Ruth Mountain, traverse glacier and snow south and west to approximate 6500 ft, then ascend talus and snow through southwest gully to summit. Route involves navigating a horizontal crevasse near the top of the glacier, aiming for notch on southwest ridgeline at 6600 ft, then south through glacier's west face. Final summit push is a 100-foot Class 4 gully with mostly good rock.

Pitch 1 (5.10-): starts with a thin corner crack (~5.8) protected by small cams; after ~35 ft, bolted climbing leads to a ledge, then a short, well-protected 5.10 section reaches the first anchors. Pitch 2 (5.9-): enjoyable slabby climbing above leads to the top of the wall.
Face climbing builds to a constriction (crux) and small roof with great holds; hard sections can be bypassed. Sits in the shade all day with excellent views from the anchors.

moves.value: West side, left of a large overhanging feature
moves.from: Located west side, left of a large overhanging feature.

beta_new: From a backcountry camp near Indian Pass (5,000 ft) on the Pacific Crest Trail, climbers leave the trail and head up bushy hillside on the peak's southwest/south slopes; the terrain opens up above the brush into Class 2 talus and boulder slopes. The line trends up onto the west ridge and follows it toward the summit block. The ridge holds twin summits close in height -- most parties stop at the west (false) summit where a register sits, but trip reports and elevation checks indicate the east summit is 15-40 feet higher and has better Class 3 scrambling; reaching it requires a short, loose, exposed corkscrew move around onto the peak's southeast face near the top.

The easiest (and only documented) line up Indian Mountain is straightforward Class 2 scrambling on open talus and heather slopes above treeline. The crux of the trip is logistical, not technical: a long approach through North Cascades National Park wilderness (Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River corridor, and the Whatcom Pass/Brush Creek/Indian Creek drainages), unbridged fords, brushy avalanche-path sections, and finally sustained off-trail cross-country travel to gain the summit ridge. The peak's defining character is its relief, rising more than 4,100 ft above Brush Creek valley in roughly one mile, so the final push feels steep even though no roped climbing is required.

The lower northeast ridge section climbs 4th-to-easy-fifth-class (5.4 max) slabs and cracks on excellent rock. It's followed by the crux upper east-face pitch, graded 5.6 X on rock described as horrible, with almost no protection - this is not a route for the average 5.6 climber, and picking the wrong line on the face can be fatal.

moves.from: A 70 m rope and a light alpine rack are needed.

beta_new: The South Ridge ascends south-facing aspect of North Peak via mixed terrain and crack systems. Hike broken rock and slabs to broad bench below the large red slab. Two main crack variations: traditional 5.4 on left, 5.6 Beckey variation in middle. Pitches are bolted at anchors (pitches 2-3) with additional slings at pitch 1. Serpentine rock sections are notably slick; helmets recommended above 6,900 ft due to rockfall hazard. Parties of 3-4 fit comfortably on small belay ledges.

South Peak (7,640 ft) is the southernmost and easiest of Ingalls Peak's three summits. The standard route ascends the north ridge/gullies from the North-South col to the summit block, where a short, exposed high-Class-3 move on solid rock gains the true summit. Scramble features solid, high-friction Jurassic peridotite throughout. Descent reverses the ascent via the same ridge/gully system. Total round trip approximately 11 miles (17.7 km) and 3,500–4,200 ft of elevation gain.

From below Home Lake the northwest face of Inner Constance comes into view. The route climbs roughly 3 pitches through a crack system over rotten, loose rock to a cave beneath an overhanging roof; the crux is building an anchor there and making an exposed, committing move out of the cave by underclinging the roof and traversing right about 10-15 ft. Several further pitches of class 4-to-low-5th climbing lead to the false summit. Protection is sparse throughout (roughly one usable placement per 20-100 ft).

From high camp on the edge of the Inspiration Glacier, the peaks can be taken in any order, but a common plan is Eldorado first (a short climb up the snow of its East Ridge to an exposed, knife-edge snow crest at the summit), then east across the Inspiration Glacier to camp at the rock col on the south side of Klawatti. From there, continue over the Klawatti Glacier and the North Klawatti Glacier to Primus, whose south side is easy snow, slabs and mostly stable talus, reaching the south ridge a short way below the top. Austera, reached from the Klawatti/Austera glacier side, has a snowy ridge between its false and true summits and then a short chimney with 4th-class to low-5th mantle moves; most parties belay it and rappel once. Klawatti is climbed from the col on its south side: cross the moat, climb a steep gully with several 4th-class moves (or two or three short low-5th pitches on the southwest buttress), then scramble loose rock and an easy ridge to the long summit; descend with a rappel back over the moat. Dorado Needle is reached from the McAllister Glacier side: gain the ridge north of the peak, then follow an exposed knife-edge ridge that is crossed au cheval to a tiny summit, where the final move is a short, awkward boulder problem up an angled crack in a steep step (about 5.7-5.9). Descend by rappel rather than re-crossing the knife edge, then return over the Inspiration and Eldorado glaciers to the car.

Begins with juggy holds and progresses through increasingly technical movement. The crux comes right before the last bolt, with an option to move right or take a recently-cleaned left-side slot finish.

moves.value: Anchor 6 ft above the final bolt, partly hidden behind small trees
moves.from: Anchors sit 6 ft above the final bolt, partly hidden behind small trees.

beta_new: A long backcountry approach (6.6+ trail miles, ~3,400 ft gain to Chetwoot Lake) followed by off-trail cross-country travel and unroped class 3 scrambling on the west and north ridges. Solid granite in places but loose talus and scree lower down; most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a camp at Big Heart or Chetwoot Lake.

The easiest way up Ives Peak is a scramble. The standard approach follows the Pacific Crest Trail / Goat Rocks crest, which runs close to the peak's western slopes, then leaves the crest at the col northwest of the peak and follows the northwest ridge and a short south-face scramble to the summit; this is unroped class 2-3 talus/scree, not a technical rock or ice route. The ridge north of the summit is rocky and wind-scoured, with a short loose section near the col, and snow lingers on the peak's flanks into early summer.

This is the only repeatable Grade VI big wall in the Pacific Northwest with bolted stainless steel anchors and portaledge bivy opportunities achievable by experienced wall climbers in 3-4 days. Climbing follows a continuous crack system featuring varied aid pitches including thin pins, rivets, hooks, and roof passages. The Fang Roof (Pitch 8) stands out as a classic pitch with hand crack free climbing through an overhang. Plan for 7 days of capsule-style climbing with portaledge camps to complete the first ascent.

This is an early-season snow climb, done when the north cirque is still filled in. The Nohokomeen Glacier runs from about 6,100 ft to 8,200 ft, is over 340 acres, and is heavily crevassed after the midpoint of its descent, so rope up. Above the glacier the headwall is the crux: it is variously described as 700 vertical feet of snow at slopes up to 60 degrees, and as a sustained 50-55 degrees for about 800 feet with steeper steps. Most parties simul-climb it, taking turns kicking steps, with a rope over the shoulder for the bergschrund; winter parties have pitched it out with pickets, cams, nuts and screws through a mixed cliff band. The bergschrund is the main obstacle and normally goes on a single bridge on the left side. Above, exit onto the ridge and finish along a narrow, corniced summit ridge with rocky drops — the last few hundred feet are the most exposed of the route.

moves.from: From the East Bank Trailhead follow the East Bank Trail roughly 8 miles to the May Creek camp, then leave the trail and climb about 3 miles of steep, bushy, cliff-banded forest — cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are passed on game trails — to reach snowline near 4,800-5,000 ft and a camp either on the flats around 5,200 ft below the glacier or higher on the glacier itself around 7,400 ft.

beta_new: From the upper basin east of Jack, climb moraine and snow to the serrated rock col just east of the Southeast Ridge. Cross a little west of its lowest point; elsewhere the far side is too steep. Downclimb roughly 250 ft of broken rock and snow gullies onto the glacier, then traverse to its narrow northern part and find a way through. The glacier is chaotic and usually only goes in early summer. The first party had to leave it for snow and rock on the buttress to its right, then traversed back across the ice to the notch below the summit. From the notch, finish as for the North Ridge. Allow about six hours from camp.
Bolts to anchors. Real short route, great for teaching new climbers.

Modern parties climbing the fuller/harder version of the same buttress rate it Grade V, 5.8, AI2: a short approach leads to loose lower slabs, then thousands of feet of near-vertical vegetation (alder, turf, heather), a 5.5-5.8 rock band to a ~7,100 ft bivy, an exposed snow arête, and a short ice pitch to the summit ridge.
